headline: Real face.
Fake words.
stories.body: AI can make real people appear to say things they never said.
stories.sourceType: Current platform policy, not an independent audit
stories.evidence: YouTube requires disclosure of realistic AI content, including making a real person appear to say or do something they did not do.
stories.limits: The card describes a capability and disclosure policy. It does not claim all AI content is deceptive or that every misleading clip is labeled.
stories.alt: Royal blue Story with large white headline: Real face. Fake words. Supporting text: AI can make real people appear to say things they never said. Source: YouTube AI-disclosure policy, checked November 12, 2026. The Daily Nun masthead.

headline: Mad?
That's
the hook.
stories.body: Rage bait is designed to turn anger into clicks and engagement.
stories.sourceTitle: The Oxford Word of the Year 2025 is rage bait
stories.evidence: Oxford defines rage bait as online content deliberately designed to provoke anger or outrage, typically to increase traffic or engagement.
stories.limits: This defines a tactic. It does not identify a particular post as intentional bait, prove an algorithm always rewards anger, or imply all anger is misplaced.
stories.alt: Off-white Story with large dark headline: Mad? That's the hook. Supporting text: Rage bait is designed to turn anger into clicks and engagement. Source: Oxford Languages, Word of the Year 2025. The Daily Nun masthead.

headline: Review
or ad?
stories.body: YouTube requires creators to disclose sponsorships and other commercial relationships.
stories.sourceTitle: Add branded content restrictions & disclosure labels
stories.sourceType: Current platform policy, not legal advice or an enforcement audit
stories.evidence: YouTube instructs creators featuring branded content, sponsorships, endorsements or other commercial relationships to select the paid-promotion setting, which adds a disclosure label.
stories.limits: The statement is limited to YouTube's rule. Sponsored content can be accurate; a missing label is not proof of a secret deal. It does not describe every platform's rules.
stories.alt: Dark Story with large white headline: Review or ad? Supporting text: YouTube requires creators to disclose sponsorships and other commercial relationships. Source: YouTube branded-content policy, checked November 12, 2026. The Daily Nun masthead.

headline: Your feed
is the
front page.
stories.body: 43% of U.S. adults ages 18–29 regularly get news on Instagram.
stories.sourceTitle: Social Media and News Fact Sheet
stories.sourceType: Nationally representative survey / self-reported news habits
stories.evidence: The fact sheet's demographic table reports 43% for regular Instagram news consumption among U.S. adults ages 18–29.
stories.measurement: Survey conducted August 24–30, 2026 among 5,166 U.S. adults overall. The 43% denominator is U.S. adults ages 18–29, not Instagram users and not all members of Gen Z. Platform users were asked whether they regularly get news there. The estimate does not measure news accuracy or exclusive reliance on Instagram.
stories.limits: The headline is an editorial metaphor. The survey does not establish that Instagram is this group's main or only news source. Sample size is for the full survey, not the age subgroup.
stories.alt: Off-white Story with large dark headline: Your feed is the front page. Supporting text: 43% of U.S. adults ages 18 to 29 regularly get news on Instagram. Source: Pew Research Center survey, August 24 to 30, 2026. The Daily Nun masthead.

headline: Your fave
is the
news desk.
stories.body: 38% of U.S. adults ages 18–29 regularly get news from influencers.
stories.sourceType: Nationally representative survey / self-reported news habits
stories.evidence: Pew reports that 38% of U.S. adults ages 18–29 say they regularly get news from news influencers on social media.
stories.measurement: Survey conducted August 18–24, 2025. Denominator: U.S. adults ages 18–29. News influencers were defined as individuals with a large social-media following who often post about news or political or social issues. Only respondents reporting social-media news use were asked the influencer question; Pew reports the estimate for the age population. This is not a new 2026 finding.
stories.limits: The headline is an editorial metaphor. These are self-reported habits, not proof that creators are more or less accurate than journalists. 'Ages 18–29' is not identical to the entire Gen Z population.
stories.alt: Royal blue Story with large white headline: Your fave is the news desk. Supporting text: 38% of U.S. adults ages 18 to 29 regularly get news from influencers. Source: Pew Research Center survey, August 18 to 24, 2025. The Daily Nun masthead.

headline: Same app.
Different
feeds.
stories.body: TikTok says watch time, likes, and other interactions help shape recommendations.
stories.sourceType: Platform explanation, not an independent algorithm audit
stories.evidence: TikTok describes user interactions, content information, and user information as recommendation factors. It says interactions, including watch time, generally receive greater weight for most users and that feeds remain unique to each person.
stories.limits: The card attributes the explanation to TikTok. It does not establish that personalization causes polarization or that feeds contain only one viewpoint.
stories.alt: Dark Story with large white headline: Same app. Different feeds. Supporting text: TikTok says watch time, likes, and other interactions help shape recommendations. Source: TikTok Help Center, checked November 12, 2026. The Daily Nun masthead.
